Senses.Explanation: Right then and there: a temporal expression marking something as occurring without an intervening interval. Shanglan Shun's verse says accumulated ignorance disappears right then; the Five Lamps narrator says Zhitian awakens on the spot when shown the blowing-a-hair case. Huangbo Xiyun uses it for the time of becoming clear without retaining a mark of clarity, while Linji Yixuan uses it for being without further business after turning the light back and recognizing no difference from the patriarchs and buddhas. Huqiu Shaolong says that if listeners trust the presented mind-settling scene, the mind is settled right then. Wuyi Yuanlai attaches the expression to one thought not arising, Miyin to the ice-like disappearance of a raised repentance case, Xuedou Chongxian to a mirror distinguishing beautiful and ugly as soon as it is set up, and the Yongzheng Emperor to a selected saying and discriminating consciousness shattering on the spot. The Zen record prizes the compressed timing, but the word itself remains a temporal modifier: it does not by itself name a teaching, a prescribed exercise, or a distinct temporal entity.

Senses.Explanation: Meeting the occasion means answering or acting aptly at the live trigger-point of an encounter. The phrase can introduce a request—“with one phrase meeting the occasion, please speak the teaching” (一句當機請師說法)—or appraise an immediate response. Feiyin Tongrong strikes the staff and says, “freed through on the occasion; it is no other thing” (當機透脫，更非別物). Yuanwu's verse says that buddhas and patriarchs “value what is ready-made when meeting the occasion” (佛祖當機貴見成) and immediately calls for someone to come before the assembly and settle doubt. Thus the corpus bends a general word for apt timing toward the live occasion of encounter, question, answer, and response.

Chan records repeatedly couple it with results said to occur without going elsewhere: liberation 'right where it is,' arising right there and appearing wherever one goes, quiescence right there, and the place of teaching right there. Senses.Explanation: Miss it face to face is a sharp encounter verdict: the requested matter is already present in the exchange, yet the questioner or audience passes it by at the very moment of meeting it. Jingshan Zhice answers the question why the Tiantai master is beneath his questioner's feet with the headword itself. Sanshan Denglai likewise gives it as the answer when a hypothetical interlocutor calls his reply worlds apart, while Yuanwu Keqin uses it as his answer for the Yunmen house. The phrase also warns an audience against losing the immediate event. Tianyin Yuanxiu says the monastery's timber, tiles, and stones are already turning the teaching wheel and tells the assembly not to miss it face to face; Liao'an Qingyu asks why half the audience still does so despite an overt explanation. In another Yuanwu address, even Yunmen and Muzhou are judged to have missed face to face, so the verdict is not reserved for novices.

Senses.Explanation: To miss something face-to-face is to fail to recognize what is directly present; speakers apply the warning to a person, ordinary sights, a staff, and an encounter before the assembly. The phrase occurs as a verdict, a warning, and an author's acknowledgment. Meixi Du pairs two kinds of people: those who stand out shoulder it directly, while those confused about the head and recognizing a shadow miss it face-to-face (超群拔萃的，直下荷擔；迷頭認影的，當面錯過). In a letter he says that on first meeting a correspondent he did not recognize the correspondent's freedom and literary quality, “truly what is called missing it face-to-face” (誠所謂當面錯過也); this is the corpus's only formula using “what is called” for the term. Boshan Wuyi says, after asking whether anyone can assess the value of what he has presented, “one still must not miss it face-to-face” (也不可當面錯過). Elsewhere Boshan lists “rice comes from grain, soup from water, and a nun is a woman,” then says “do not miss it face-to-face” (飯是米做底、湯是水做底、師姑是女人做底，切莫當面錯過). Yunxi's record places the warning after “kites fly and fish leap; mountains stand and water flows” (鳶飛魚躍，山峙水流，切莫當面錯過). Panlong calls on his staff to bring news to the assembly, warns them not to miss it face-to-face, raises the staff, and asks whether they understand. The exact phrase is attested.

Senses.Explanation: Tao Yuanming is the poet whom these records recognize through wine, chrysanthemums, and his decision to return home. Masters make that literary figure work in public speech: 'if it were Tao Yuanming, he would frown and go home' dismisses a labored formulation, while other addresses pair his return with withdrawal from a crowded or defiled scene. He is therefore a pre-Chan figure as deployed by Chan speakers, not a lineage master and not merely a biographical name.
